connection: Session 30 covered Scoped lifetime, previewing ASP.NET Core's per-request scoping. This session studies the real Parm.Practice.WebApi/Program.cs scaffold, mirrored verbatim in PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Program.cs: it calls AddControllers()/MapControllers() against zero controller classes. This session writes the first one.
objectives: Read PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Program.cs and confirm, by inspection, that AddControllers()/MapControllers() are wired up with no Controllers/ directory and no controller classes anywhere in the project -- a real, verified gap, not a hypothetical.
Write ClockEntriesController, the project's first real controller, exposing an HTTP endpoint over the real IClockEntryService.
Explain why a controller action's parameters and return type form a DTO boundary distinct from the domain's ClockEntry/Employee types.
Confirm MapControllers() now has at least one real route to map, by calling the new endpoint.

visuals.title: The real, verified gap
visuals.explanation: builder.Services.AddControllers(); ... app.MapControllers(); -- both real lines exist in Parm.Practice.WebApi/Program.cs today, with zero [ApiController] classes anywhere in the project for them to map.

visuals.title: A controller action is the missing piece
visuals.explanation: [HttpPost] public IActionResult ClockIn(int employeeId) gives MapControllers() something real to route requests to -- the first controller this real project has ever had.

visuals.title: The action's parameters are the HTTP boundary, not the domain boundary
visuals.explanation: A controller action receives request data (route values, query strings, request bodies) -- it is not the same thing as calling IClockEntryService.ClockIn(int employeeId) directly from C# code.

visuals.title: One request, routed to one action, calling the real service
visuals.explanation: POST /employees/1/clock-in -> ClockEntriesController.ClockIn(1) -> the real, unmodified IClockEntryService.ClockIn(1).

preQuiz.prompt: Why does the real Parm.Practice.WebApi project currently have zero working HTTP endpoints, despite calling AddControllers() and MapControllers()?
options: Those two calls only wire up the infrastructure FOR controllers -- MapControllers() maps whatever [ApiController]-attributed classes it finds, and the real project has never had any
AddControllers() and MapControllers() are broken in this version of ASP.NET Core
The project uses minimal APIs instead, which are incompatible with MapControllers()
preQuiz.explanation: This is confirmed by inspecting the real project directly -- the DI/routing infrastructure is present and correctly configured; only the controllers themselves are missing.

preQuiz.prompt: What does ClockEntriesController.ClockIn(int employeeId) actually call to perform the real work?
options: The real, unmodified IClockEntryService.ClockIn(int employeeId) -- the controller is a thin HTTP-facing wrapper around logic that already exists and is already tested
A new, duplicate implementation of the clock-in logic written specifically for the controller
preQuiz.explanation: This is the whole point of Sessions 5-19's interface-based design: the controller is new, but the logic it calls into is the same real, already-tested ClockEntryService.

preQuiz.prompt: Is a controller action's int employeeId parameter (bound from the URL) the same thing as calling IClockEntryService.ClockIn(employeeId) directly in C# code?
options: Not exactly -- the controller parameter is bound from an HTTP request (route value, query string, or body) by ASP.NET Core's model binding, THEN passed to the real ClockIn method; the HTTP boundary and the domain method call are two distinct steps
Yes -- they are identical in every respect
No -- controller actions cannot call domain services at all
preQuiz.explanation: This distinction matters for Session 34's DTO/validation discussion: HTTP requests need explicit binding and validation before their values can be trusted as valid domain method arguments.

concept.title: The real, verified gap
paragraphs: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Program.cs mirrors Parm.Practice.WebApi/Program.cs verbatim: builder.Services.AddControllers(); wires up controller-related services, and app.MapControllers(); tells ASP.NET Core's routing to map any [ApiController]-attributed classes it discovers -- but there is no Controllers/ directory anywhere in the project, and zero such classes exist.

This is real and current, not a hypothetical scenario -- confirmed by inspecting both the real practice-07092026 repository and this course's own PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web project before this session's lab.

concept.title: ClockEntriesController: the first real controller
paragraphs: A minimal controller action exposing the real, already-tested IClockEntryService.ClockIn over HTTP -- new code, but calling into logic Sessions 5 and 19 already built and tested.
[ApiController] plus a route attribute is what makes this class discoverable by MapControllers(); nothing about IClockEntryService itself needs to change for this to work.

concept.title: The HTTP boundary is a separate step from the domain call
paragraphs: Before ClockIn(int employeeId) ever runs, ASP.NET Core's model binding has already parsed employeeId out of the URL segment {employeeId} and converted it to an int -- a step Session 34 studies more closely when it can fail (a non-numeric segment, for instance).

This is why controller actions are described as a boundary: everything on one side (HTTP requests, routing, model binding) is new to this session; everything on the other side (IClockEntryService, ClockEntry, the real domain) is unchanged from Sessions 5-29.

lab.objective: Add ClockEntriesController as the real project's first controller, and confirm MapControllers() now routes a real HTTP request to it.
lab.startingCondition: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Program.cs already calls AddControllers()/MapControllers() with zero controllers, mirroring the real, current Parm.Practice.WebApi project exactly.
steps: Confirm, by searching the project, that no Controllers/ directory or [ApiController] class currently exists.
Add Controllers/ClockEntriesController.cs with a ClockIn action calling the real IClockEntryService.ClockIn.
Run the WebApi host and send a POST request to the new route, confirming a successful response.
Confirm the underlying ClockEntryRepository now has a new open ClockEntry for that employee, proving the controller genuinely reached the real domain logic.
lab.expectedBehavior: Before the lab, no route exists for clocking in over HTTP. After adding ClockEntriesController, the POST request succeeds and a new open ClockEntry is created through the same real ClockEntryService used by the console app.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

Write the project's first real controller, filling the gap MapControllers() has been waiting on.

commit: session-32: teach aspnet core requests routing and dto boundaries
review: The real, current zero-controller gap is confirmed by inspection before any code is written, not assumed.
ClockEntriesController calls the real, unmodified IClockEntryService rather than duplicating its logic.
The HTTP boundary (model binding, routing) is explicitly distinguished from the domain method call it eventually makes.
The full test suite passes, and the new endpoint is confirmed working end to end.

postQuiz.prompt: If PayrollService were resolved inside a new controller action today, without any other changes, what real bug from the source WebApi would surface?
options: The real, latent missing-IEmployeeService-registration bug -- PayrollService's constructor requires IEmployeeService, which PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Program.cs (mirroring the real WebApi) never registers, so resolution would throw InvalidOperationException
Nothing -- PayrollService resolves without issue in the WebApi host
A compile error, not a runtime error
postQuiz.explanation: This is exactly the bug Session 34 discovers and fixes -- Session 33 deliberately used IClockEntryService, which IS fully registered, so this particular controller avoids the bug; Session 34 confronts it directly.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does ClockEntriesController.ClockIn accept int employeeId as a route parameter rather than, say, a full ClockEntry object in the request body?
options: Clocking in only requires an identity (which employee); ClockEntry's ClockIn timestamp is set by the server (DateTime.Now, inside the real ClockEntryService.ClockIn), not supplied by the client -- the route parameter matches exactly what the operation actually needs from the caller
ASP.NET Core does not support request bodies
ClockEntry cannot be deserialized from JSON
postQuiz.explanation: This mirrors the real ClockEntryService.ClockIn(int employeeId) signature exactly -- the controller's parameter list is deliberately no wider than the domain method it calls.

postQuiz.prompt: Was writing ClockEntriesController itself a change to any existing, real, tested code?
options: No -- it is entirely new code; IClockEntryService, ClockEntryService, and every existing test remain completely unmodified
Yes -- IClockEntryService needed a new HTTP-specific method
Yes -- ClockEntry's constructor needed to change
postQuiz.explanation: This is deliberate: the controller is additive, calling into the exact same real, already-verified domain logic every earlier session already tested.

reflections: Why did MapControllers() compile and run successfully for 31 sessions with zero controllers to map, without ever producing an error?
What would you need to add to ClockEntriesController for it to also expose Clockout and CalculateTotalHours over HTTP?
How does keeping ClockEntriesController's action parameters narrow (just employeeId) protect it from becoming coupled to internal domain details that might change?
whatBreaks: Forgetting the [ApiController] attribute (or a valid route) on a new controller class means MapControllers() still will not discover it -- ASP.NET Core needs both the attribute and app.MapControllers() together to route requests to it. Calling PayrollService instead of IClockEntryService from a new controller action today would surface the real, still-unfixed missing-IEmployeeService-registration bug before Session 34 formally addresses it.
summary: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/Program.cs -- mirroring the real, current Parm.Practice.WebApi/Program.cs -- calls AddControllers()/MapControllers() against zero controller classes, a real and verified gap, not a hypothetical one. This session's lab writes ClockEntriesController, the project's first real controller, calling directly into the same real, already-tested IClockEntryService every earlier session built -- the HTTP boundary (routing, model binding) is new; the domain logic it reaches is not.
